text:
The stock dropped 1.7% today and has fallen nearly 16% over two weeks, a move that tracks closely with oil prices weakening from $107 to $99.50 per barrel over that same span. Refineries are running at 94.5% capacity with ample crude and product inventories, suggesting the refining margin—the profit refiners make by turning crude into gasoline and diesel—is under pressure as crude gets cheaper but demand remains moderate. Yesterday's sharp 8.6% drop coincided with news that Democrats are preparing investigations into energy policy decisions, which adds political uncertainty to the refining sector's already challenging economics.

The two-week decline reflects a broader squeeze on refiner profitability: crude prices are falling while refinery utilization stays high, narrowing the gap between input and output costs. Oil demand remains uncertain despite executives' talk of a "demand decade" ahead, leaving room for crude inventories to build if consumption disappoints.
